ety.text: From anash + kaloj, literally meaning 'to pass on the side'.
From albanian "ar" meaning gold and "vëndi" meaning land or place. The meaning of the name is therefore "golden land".
A compound of bërth, a variant of bathë + amë (“mother”), literally conveying the meaning of 'mother of the fruit'.

Derived from Greek σάκος (sákos), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), most likely from Semitic. A formation with the enforcement of the fricative ‘s’ into an affricate, similar to ca.
Similar to cakël, an elementary formation from cak, meaning a result of slicing and dicing in tiny pieces. Encountered in southern Gheg dialect, Shpat region. Used only in plural.
Derivative of dal (“exit, protrude, jut out”), contaminated with dalloj (“make out, distinguish”).

s.g: a male given name from Arabic, equivalent to English David

ety.text: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish داوود (dāwūd), from Arabic دَاوُود (dāwūd), from Biblical Hebrew דָּוִד (dāwīḏ).

x: Vëllai i saj është një djalë shumë joshës.
Me ty o djalë sa netet kalova

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *dela, from *dʰeh₁-l-os, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-l- (compare Latvian dêls (“son”), Latin filius (“son”), Old English delu (“teat”), Old Armenian դալ (dal)), from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Originally a neuter noun, as it appears in Buzuku's Meshari.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin deliberāre.
From (pre-)Proto-Albanian *źinu (“bosom”), from Proto-Indo-European *s(e)i-nu (“curved body part”). Similar development to Latin sinus (“breast; curve”).
From Greek γειτονία (geitonía). Possibly from gji + tonë

s.g: A municipality in Fier County, Albania, now part of Lushnjë.
A municipality in Tirana County, Albania, now part of Kavajë.
A municipality in Gjirokastër County, Albania, now part of Gjirokastër.
A municipality in Shkodër County, Albania, now part of Shkodër.

ety.text: From kap (“I grab, catch, grip”) + -th (diminutive suffix); the former from Proto-Albanian *kapa, from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Cognate with Lithuanian kāpas (“grave”), kopà (“dune”), Latvian kãpa (“dune”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *kapja, from Proto-Indo-European *kop(H)- (compare Lithuanian kàpti, Ancient Greek κόπτω (kóptō)).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *kapja, from Proto-Indo-European *kop(H)- (compare Lithuanian kàpti, Ancient Greek κόπτω (kóptō)).

s.g: of, or relating to the subjunctive mood

ety.text: Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *lupus cervulus, from lupus cervārius (“lynx”) (compare French loup-cervier, Italian lupo cerviero, Romansh luf tscherver), from Latin lupus + cervārius < cervus. Doublet of rrëqebull (“lynx”).

s.g: (it/they) drip(s) (liquids/water from a window, ground/soil, etc.) (third person sg/pl)
(it/they) squeak(s), squeal(s), crack(s) (associated with the noise of a door, window, wheel) (third person sg/pl)
(it/they) need(s), miss(es); (it/they) lack(s) (someone or something), cry(cries) for (someone/something) (third person sg/pl)
to mourn, cry over (because of a loss or death of someone); to cry over (something (such as past time, money))
to do (it) perfectly, master (something specific); to have a talent (for a specific profession/work; playing an instrument)

ety.text: From variant qanj, from older klanj, from Proto-Albanian *klaunja, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (compare English loud, Czech slout (“to be called, have a reputation”), Greek κλαίω (klaío, “to weep, sob”)).

tpl.gloss: to be called, have a reputation

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *śter-, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread, scatter, bring down”).

s.g: weaning pen for lambs and kids
large basket for carrying hay or straw
crib, shed, or chest for storing corn
long-term storage pit covered with oak and chestnut branches

ety.text: Alteration of variant cark, from Proto-Albanian *tsarka, from *ḱorH-ko-, o-grade from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to bind, plait”). More at thur. The Greek and Aromanian/Romanian loanwords were borrowed from the variant cark.
From earlier ungël, borrowed through Vulgar Latin *aunculo or Vulgar Latin *aunclus, from Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”). cf. Romanian unchi.

Borrowed from English winch. Itself from Middle English wynche, from Old English winċe, from Proto-Germanic *winkijǭ, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *weng- (“to bow, bend, arch, curve”). Compare Serbo-Croatian vinč.
Ultimately from Byzantine Greek βόωψ (bóōps), *βῶψ (*bôps), accusative βῶπα (bôpa). Compare Italian vopa, Greek γόπα (gópa).

s.g: banquet, feast, big party with many invitees

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *tši, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid. Cognate to Hittite 𒆪𒀉 (/⁠kuit⁠/), Greek τί (tí), Latin quid.
